title: The Cynic’s Guide to Church
text:
What this is
This is a class for people who have complicated, honest, unresolved feelings about the church.
Not a debate. Not a recovery program. Not Sunday school. Not a space where you’ll be told to forgive faster, doubt less, or look on the bright side.
It’s a space where you can name what you’ve experienced…the good and the bad…examine it honestly, and figure out what to do with it.
Over eight sessions, we’ll hold two things at the same time without letting either one cancel out the other:
Both are true. The goal is to wrestle with that tension in an honest way.

title: The Cynic’s Guide to Church
text:
Who this is for
This class is for:

Current attenders who are struggling with aspects of their church experience
People who have stepped back or left and aren’t sure what to do next
Longtime churchgoers who feel disillusioned but can’t fully articulate why
Skeptics and returnees who are somewhere in between
Church lovers who are consistently lifted up by their church experience

You don’t have to have it figured out.

Before you begin

This class was built for a specific community, but the questions belong to anyone who has ever loved the church, been hurt by it, or both.

title: Ground Rules
text:
Why we make agreements together
Group norms are chosen, handed down, or emerge unconciously.
In this class, we want to chose our norms. The list below reflects the results of our Session 1 conversation: “What do I need from this room in order to tell the truth?”
These have been updated based on our conversation.

title: Ground Rules
text:
The covenant

The Cynic’s Guide to Church — Group Covenant

What is shared here stays here. What you learn about yourself is yours to take. Stories stay. Lessons leave. You can talk about what you’re learning. You should not talk outside this room about who said what. Note: you can ask permission from someone to share
You can share your experience without being the spokesperson for everyone who has had experiences like yours. You are not the representative of “all abuse survivors” or “all evangelicals” or “all people who left.” You speak only for yourself.
We are not here to fix everyone. We are here to understand each other. This is not a debate. The goal is listening and processing, not preparing our rebuttal while someone else is speaking.
You can pass. Always. On anything. Silence is participation. You do not have to share to be here. Nobody should feel pressure to disclose anything they’re not ready to share.
Speak from your own experience. Use “I” language. “I felt…” not “People like that always…” “In my experience…” not “The church never…”
Questions are welcome. You don’t have to resolve them to ask them. You can process out loud Sitting with a hard question is not the same as failing to answer it. Both belong here. If you feel uncomfortable discussing something in class, let me know. I promise you will not offend me.
The facilitator is not perfect. If you feel something is in error, you have 100% permission to bring it up. I, as your facilitator also reserve the right to say, “I don’t know”…a lot
Be as honest as you are able. Performative positivity…saying what you think you should feel..is as unhelpful here as unchecked venting. We want what is actually true for you.
Assume positive intent. Most people in this room are trying. When something lands wrong, say so…but assume accident before malice.
Be humble. There are multiple sides to any and everything.
Scripture First We will look to the Bible for primary guidance
Help each other Gently hold each other accountable to this set of norms

title: Ground Rules
text:
A few words on confidentiality
Confidentiality is the most important agreement on this list, and it deserves more than a bullet point.
What confidentiality means here:

The specific things people share in this room: their stories, their pain, their doubts…stay in this room…unless the owner give permission.
You may share with a spouse or close friend that you’re processing something, without naming what anyone else said.
No gossip. You may not share someone’s story as an anecdote. You may not use what you’ve heard here as data points in arguments elsewhere.

title: Session 1
text:
The Dress



The dress — what colors do you see?


Source: Wikipedia — The dress · Photo originally by Cecilia Bleasdale · CC BY-SA 4.0



What the Facebook video and the dress reveal
Some key takeaways:
We all bring different experiences, mental models, and internal logics to everything we encounter. That is not a flaw in how humans work. It is just how humans work. The dress makes this visible in a way that is almost impossible to argue with, because it is happening right in front of you in real time. Two people, same image, genuinely different experiences. Neither is lying. Neither is wrong. Their visual systems are processing the same information through different prior frameworks and arriving at different conclusions.
The deeper point is this: sometimes those internal models – those priors – make it virtually impossible to see a set of stimuli any other way. It is not stubbornness. It is not stupidity. The prior is doing its job so efficiently that the alternative interpretation is genuinely not available to the person looking. That is worth sitting with, because it applies directly to how we experience the church.
Even where there is a truth to be found, what we experience is always shaped by what we bring to the experience. The sermon clip made this visible. Same three minutes of preaching. Some people found it moving. Some found it manipulative. Some felt both at once. None of those responses were random – they were the entirely predictable output of each person’s history, wounds, hopes, and prior exposure filtering the same inputs.
This has a practical implication that is easy to miss. If we cannot even perceive what someone else is perceiving – if the blue-and-black dress genuinely looks white and gold to us – then trying to argue or debate them into seeing it our way is largely futile. And yet that is often what we do with church. We present evidence. We make arguments. We get frustrated when people do not come around. The dress suggests that the problem may not be the evidence.
What can actually help is trying to understand what the other person is seeing, and why. That approach does not require you to abandon your own perspective. It does not validate everything someone else believes. But it opens a door that argument keeps closed. It invites conversation rather than entrenching positions. It treats the other person’s experience as real data rather than error to be corrected. And occasionally – not always, but occasionally – it helps us see something we genuinely could not see before.
That is one of the most valuable things that happens in community. Not agreement. Not uniformity. The exposure to perspectives that your own prior history would never have generated on its own.
The Facebook video adds one more layer. The same content – same words, same speaker, same delivery – can produce a range of reactions from genuine inspiration to profound discomfort, and everything between. When that happens, “you should feel inspired by this” or “you shouldn’t be bothered by that” is not a useful response. It does not reflect how perception actually works, and it tends to shut people down rather than draw them out.
What is more useful is curiosity. “I wonder why we experienced that so differently” is not a concession. It is an invitation. It is the beginning of the kind of conversation that actually builds something between people.



Carrying this into the rest of the class
This is the foundation everything else in this class rests on. Before we talk about authority, or harm, or what the church is supposed to be, we need to understand that every person in this room is looking through a lens they did not entirely choose. That includes you. It includes the facilitator. It includes the people who built the institutions we are examining.
That does not mean every perspective is equally accurate, or that nothing is true, or that real harm did not happen. It means the conversation requires something more than competing assertions. It requires genuine curiosity about what others are seeing, and enough humility to consider that our own lens might be revealing some things while hiding others.
The question to carry into Session 2:

What experiences, relationships, or ways of thinking are most shaping the way you currently see or interact with the church?

You do not have to answer it out loud. But it is worth knowing your own answer before we go further.

title: Session 2
section: Before we get to anything else
text:
Before we get to anything else
Try this. Read each of these sentences and ask yourself what the word “church” is actually pointing to:

“Where do you go to church?”
“Church starts at 10.”
“We haven’t been to church lately.”
“That church has great preaching.”
“We’re looking for a church with a good youth program.”

In the first sentence, “church” is a place. In the second, it’s an event with a start time. In the third, it’s a habit or practice. In the fourth, it’s an organization with qualities. In the fifth, it’s a service provider you might choose or not choose.
That’s five different meanings in five sentences, and we use them all without thinking twice.
So when we say “the church hurt me” or “the church changed my life” – what are we actually talking about? That question turns out to matter a lot. This session is an attempt to answer it carefully.

title: Session 2
text:
The word itself
The Greek word behind our English “church” is ekklesia (ek-klay-SEE-ah). It’s usually translated as church, assembly, or congregation.
Here is the first thing worth knowing: this word was not invented by Christians. In ordinary Greek, ekklesia referred to an assembly of people gathered together. That’s all it meant. When a first-century Christian heard ekklesia, their mental picture was not a building with a sanctuary, pulpit, pews, staff, programs, and Sunday services. It was much closer to a people, an assembly, a gathered community.
The second thing worth knowing is that our English word “church” does not actually come from ekklesia at all. It comes through Germanic languages from a different Greek word, kyriakon, meaning “belonging to the Lord.”



Language
Word
Root




English
church
kyriakon


Scottish
kirk
kyriakon


German
Kirche
kyriakon


English (academic)
ecclesiastical
ekklesia



So when you read “the church at Corinth,” the underlying word is not the ancestor of our English word “church.” It is ekklesia, which just means assembly or congregation. That does not make “church” a bad translation because after centuries of Christian use, the word carries the communal meaning. But knowing the Greek history can correct some of the baggage we unconsciously attach to the English.

title: Session 2
text:
Ekklesia before Christianity
The word has a history that predates Jesus entirely. It appears throughout the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, where it often translates the Hebrew word qahal, meaning an assembly or congregation.
Deuteronomy 9:10 refers to Israel assembled before God: “on the day of the assembly.” The Greek there uses ekklesia. Deuteronomy 23 repeatedly speaks of entering the “assembly of the LORD” – again using ekklesia in the Greek translation.
So there were really two backgrounds informing how first-century Christians would have heard this word. From the Greek and Roman world, it suggested an assembly of citizens or people. From the Jewish and Old Testament world, it evoked the assembled congregation of God’s people. That combination becomes important as we move through the New Testament.

title: Session 2
text:
Jesus uses the word
Ekklesia is strikingly rare in the Gospels. It appears only in Matthew, and only twice.
Matthew 16:18

“I will build my church…”

In Greek: oikodomeso mou ten ekklesian.
Jesus does not say “I will build my religious institutions.” The object being built is his ekklesia, his people, his assembly. And notice the possessive – “my church.” The church belongs to Christ. That is already a significant claim.
Matthew 18:17

“Tell it to the church…”

Here ekklesia is more concrete. This is not simply the universal body of all Christians. It is a recognizable community of believers who are capable of hearing a dispute and responding to it. A specific group of people who know each other.
This gives us a tension worth sitting with. The church is both a theological reality and an actual community of actual people. Both are true in the New Testament at the same time.

title: Session 2
text:
Acts shows us something fascinating
Acts provides one of the clearest demonstrations that ekklesia did not inherently mean “Christian church.” Look at what happens in Acts 19, during the riot in Ephesus.
Acts 19:32: “The assembly was in confusion…”
Acts 19:39: The city clerk says the matter should be settled “in a legal assembly.”
Acts 19:41: “After he had said this, he dismissed the assembly.”
The word Luke uses in all three of those verses is ekklesia. This is a pagan mob and an official civic gathering. Luke is obviously not saying “the church was in confusion.” He is saying the assembly was in confusion. The context determines what kind of assembly is being described.
Earlier in Acts, Stephen refers to Israel gathered in the wilderness as an ekklesia (Acts 7:38). So the same word can describe Israel in the Old Testament, a pagan mob, a civic assembly, and the community of Jesus followers – all depending on context.

title: Session 2
section: Then Christianity fills the word with new meaning
text:
Then Christianity fills the word with new meaning
Once Acts begins describing the community formed around Jesus, ekklesia appears constantly.
Acts 5:11 – “Great fear seized the whole church…”
Acts 8:1 – “…a great persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem…”
Acts 8:3 – “Saul began to destroy the church.”
That last one deserves a second look. Saul was not destroying buildings. He was entering houses and dragging believers away. So what was “the church” that Saul was attacking? People. That is what the church is.

title: Session 2
text:
The different scales of ekklesia
One of the most revealing things about the New Testament’s use of ekklesia is the range of scales it covers.
The church in a particular city
This is extremely common. “The church in Jerusalem” (Acts 11:22). “The church of God in Corinth” (1 Corinthians 1:2). “The church of the Thessalonians” (1 Thessalonians 1:1). “The church in Cenchreae” where Phoebe served (Romans 16:1).
Notice that Paul does not write “To Corinth Community Church.” He writes to God’s ekklesia that is in Corinth. That is a subtly different thing – the church does not belong to the city. It belongs to God and happens to be located there.
The church in someone’s house
This may be even more revealing. Romans 16:5: “Greet also the church that meets at their house.” 1 Corinthians 16:19: Aquila and Priscilla have “the church that meets at their house.” Colossians 4:15: “Nympha and the church in her house.” Philemon 2: “the church that meets in your home.”
Ekklesia can describe a specific gathering of Christians meeting in a house. So we already have multiple scales – house, city, larger people of God – and all of them can be called ekklesia.
The church as a gathered meeting
1 Corinthians 11:18 – “When you come together as a church…”
That is fascinating language. Paul can distinguish between the people and the act of their coming together as an ekklesia. 1 Corinthians 14:23: “So if the whole church comes together…” The church actually gathers. Ekklesia is not merely an abstract spiritual identity. It is a people who assemble together and do things together.
The church as the entire people of Christ
Paul also stretches the concept far beyond any one local gathering. Ephesians 1:22-23: God appointed Christ “to be head over everything for the church, which is his body.” Ephesians 5:25: “Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.” Colossians 1:18: Christ “is the head of the body, the church.”
Here ekklesia is not one house church or the Christians in one city. It is Christ’s people collectively – people joined to Christ and therefore joined to one another.

Putting it together








Use of Ekklesia
Example

This range helps prevent two opposite mistakes.
One is “church just means the universal body of believers, so gathering is not really important.” The New Testament does not support that. Ekklesia frequently describes actual communities that actually gather.
The other is “the church is basically the Sunday service or the organization that runs it.” The New Testament does not support that either.
The ekklesia is fundamentally the people.

title: Session 2
section: One popular explanation that does not quite work
text:
One popular explanation that does not quite work
You have probably heard something like this: “Ekklesia comes from ek, meaning ‘out of,’ and kaleo, meaning ‘to call,’ so the church literally means the called-out ones.”
This is worth examining carefully, because it sounds compelling and gets repeated constantly.
The problem is Acts 19. The pagan mob rioting in Ephesus is called an ekklesia. Luke is not suggesting that the Ephesian rioters are spiritually called-out ones. By the New Testament period, the word simply meant assembly. Words mean what speakers use them to mean, not just the sum of their historical roots.
There is nothing wrong with saying that God has called his people, or that Christians are called out of darkness – 1 Peter 2:9 says exactly that. Those are true and important things. But the Greek word ekklesia does not actually establish them. That is mixing a valid theological idea with a shaky lexical argument, and it is worth knowing the difference.

title: Session 2
text:
The Temple connection
There is a bigger theological picture here that changes how we think about all of this.
The progression from Old Testament to New Testament is not primarily:
Old Testament religious building -> New Testament religious building.
It is something far more radical:
God dwells among Israel -> God dwells uniquely in Christ -> God’s Spirit dwells in his people -> those people become God’s temple, body, and household.
Under the old covenant, God’s presence was associated with a place. There were concentric boundaries: nations, then Israel, then priests, then the high priest, then the Holy of Holies. And at the center was the curtain.
That architecture communicated something almost physically: God is holy, humanity is estranged, and access is restricted.
Then Matthew records what happens at the moment of Jesus’ death:

“The curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom.” (Matthew 27:51)

That is not just a dramatic supernatural event. Hebrews makes the meaning explicit: believers now have confidence to enter God’s presence directly, by the blood of Jesus (Hebrews 10:19-22).
So Christianity does not build another Holy of Holies. Instead, Paul tells the Corinthians:

“You yourselves are God’s temple and God’s Spirit dwells in you.” (1 Corinthians 3:16)

And Peter describes Christians as “living stones” being built into a “spiritual house” (1 Peter 2:5). Ephesians 2:19-22 says believers are “being built together to become a dwelling in which God lives by his Spirit.”
The people become the building. That is the shift. God no longer primarily dwells among his people in a sacred structure. He dwells in his people by the Spirit.
The New Testament has four overlapping images for what the church is, and all of them point to this:









Image
Greek

What it communicates

Matthew 16:18
A gathered people belonging to Christ


Body of Christ
soma Christou
Ephesians 1:22-23
Joined to Christ, joined to each other

naos theou

title: Session 2
section: From restricted access to something radical
text:
From restricted access to something radical
The Temple was built around distinctions in access. Priests had access others did not. The high priest had access priests did not. Gentiles had less access than Jews. The Holy of Holies was essentially inaccessible to everyone except the high priest, once a year.
The gospel reverses that entire architecture.
Peter takes language that had been associated with Israel and the priesthood and applies it to the whole Christian community: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (1 Peter 2:9). That does not mean the New Testament church has no leaders – it clearly does. But leadership is no longer a priestly class that mediates God’s presence to ordinary believers. There is one mediator: Christ (1 Timothy 2:5).
This is why the early Christian gathering looked surprisingly simple compared to the Temple. There was no altar with priests performing sacrifices, because the sacrifice had already been offered. There was no Holy of Holies, because access had been opened. There was no sacred priestly caste, because the whole people of God are priestly. There was no geographical center toward which everyone must pilgrimage, because Christ is present with his gathered people.
The structure reflects the gospel.

title: Session 2
text:
The biblical arc
You can trace the whole story as a single line:







Stage
What it means




Eden
God with humanity


Tabernacle
God dwelling among Israel


Temple
God’s localized covenant presence


Jesus
“The Word became flesh and dwelt among us”


Church
God’s Spirit dwelling in his people


New Creation
“The dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3)



The church occupies an intermediate place in this story – between the cross and the return of Christ. We do not yet experience God’s presence as we will in the new creation. But neither are we standing on the other side of the curtain waiting for access. The Spirit has been given. Something genuinely new has happened.

title: Session 2
text:
What this means for us
If all of that is right, then the way the church exists is supposed to communicate the gospel – not just the words it speaks.
A church can verbally proclaim the priesthood of all believers while structurally making Christians into spectators. It can proclaim that God dwells in his people while functionally treating a building as the locus of God’s activity. It can proclaim reconciliation while organizing itself around demographic similarity. It can proclaim servanthood while creating celebrity leaders.
None of those contradictions are necessarily intentional. But they are worth noticing. The question is not only what our church says. It is what our church’s structure appears to say.

title: Session 2
text:
Questions worth sitting with

When you picture “the church,” what do you picture? Does anything we talked about change that?
On average, does the American Church structure demonstrate the Gospel?
How does it and how does it not?
Ephesians 2 says the church is supposed to embody reconciliation between people who were previously divided. Where have you seen that happen? Where have you seen churches reinforce those divisions instead?

Session 3 – Purpose, Functions, and Methods

title: Session 3
text:
Starting with a framework
Last session we asked what the church is. This session asks what it is for – and then traces how we got from there to what we experience today.
A useful way to think about this has three levels. The first is purpose – why does the church exist at all? The second is functions – what does it therefore need to do? The third is methods – how does it actually do those things in a specific time and place?
The distinction matters because purposes are enduring, functions flow from the purposes, and methods are contextual. Methods shift with time, culture, and circumstance. That is not a problem. The problem comes when we confuse a method with a function, or a function with the purpose itself. A lot of the frustration people carry about the church lives right in that confusion.

title: Session 3
text:
Why does the church exist?
The New Testament never gives us a clean corporate mission statement. You have to synthesize it from many different texts and images. But when you do, something like this emerges:

The church exists to become and display God’s redeemed people in Christ, and to participate in God’s mission in the world.

That is broader than “save people” or “worship God” or “make disciples.” Those are all parts of it. Here is what each piece actually means.

To display God
Paul says in Ephesians 3:10-21 that God’s intent is that “through the church, the manifold wisdom of God should be made known.”
That is an extraordinary claim. The church is not merely an organization that tells people about God. The church itself is supposed to be evidence of what God is doing. People who ordinarily would not belong together – rich and poor, different races, former enemies – become one new people reconciled to God and to one another. The community becomes part of the message.


To make disciples
This is the most familiar outward mission: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them and teaching them to obey everything I have commanded you” (Matthew 28:19-20).
Notice that Jesus does not say “make converts.” He says make disciples. Evangelism is the beginning, not the endpoint. The goal is people who actually follow Jesus – hear the gospel, believe, are baptized, are taught, and grow into obedience.


To form people into Christlikeness
Ephesians 4 may be the clearest description of what the church is supposed to produce. Christ gives apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers “to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ – until we all attain to mature manhood, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4:11-13).
Two things stand out there. First, the leaders do not actually do the ministry in Paul’s description – they equip God’s people to do it. Second, the desired output is not attendance. It is maturity. The New Testament’s scorecard for the church is something like: are these people increasingly becoming like Jesus?


To create a new kind of human community
Jesus did not simply save isolated individuals. He created a people. Peter calls Christians “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (1 Peter 2:9). Paul calls the church a body, a household, a temple, a bride.
And Jesus gives this community a defining characteristic: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another” (John 13:35). The church’s internal life becomes part of its external witness. What the community is – not only what it says – is part of the message.


To embody reconciliation
Ephesians 2 may be the most important church passage in the New Testament. Christ does not merely reconcile individuals vertically to God. He breaks down the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile and creates “one new humanity” (Ephesians 2:15).
Reconciliation with God produces reconciliation with one another. Racial, ethnic, economic, and social barriers being overcome within the Christian community are not peripheral social projects added onto the real gospel. They are supposed to be manifestations of the gospel itself – visible evidence that something has actually changed.


To bear witness to God’s kingdom
The Acts 2:42-47 community is striking. The early Christians do not merely preach a message. They become a strange kind of community: teaching, fellowship, shared meals, prayer, generosity, worship, care, and witness all woven together. And Acts says outsiders noticed. Their life together authenticated their proclamation.


To participate in God’s mission
Paul puts it this way: “God reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation… We are therefore Christ’s ambassadors” (2 Corinthians 5:18-20). The church does not exist primarily to preserve itself. It exists for God’s mission.

title: Session 3
section: What the church must therefore do
text:
What the church must therefore do
If those are the purposes, the functions follow. These are the things the church must do in some form regardless of time or place – worship, teach, form disciples, pray, share the Lord’s Supper, care for those in need, love one another, exercise gifts, reconcile, evangelize, serve, and send. They are not optional. They are what it means to be a church in any era.

title: Session 3
text:
The methods – contextual and changeable
Then there is the third layer: the specific ways a particular church in a particular time and place actually accomplishes those functions. Sermons, buildings, Sunday school, small groups, worship bands, youth ministry, staff, programs, Sunday services, mission trips, websites, budgets, denominations – all of these are methods.
Most of them exist because someone had a real problem and invented a real solution. The question is what happens over time, when the solutions accumulate and eventually start to feel like the definition of church itself.
It is worth thinking about common church practices in three rough categories. The first is things described or commanded in the New Testament – gathering, teaching, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, baptism, singing, giving, care for the poor, fellowship, mutual encouragement, evangelism, the exercise of spiritual gifts, elders, deacons, and church discipline. These are the core.
The second category is useful historical methods – large dedicated buildings, the 30-45 minute weekly sermon, Sunday morning as the primary service, seminary-trained clergy, denominations, Sunday school, the full-time senior pastor, children’s and youth ministries, the worship band. None of these are commanded in the New Testament, but they developed for real reasons and have served real purposes.
The third category is what we might call the modern consumer layer – multiple Sunday services, church branding and logos, marketing campaigns, attraction-oriented services, professional production and lighting, attendance as the primary metric of success, the pastor as CEO or celebrity, and the congregation primarily as an audience.
One important caution: “not commanded” does not mean “bad.” A church building is enormously useful. A seminary can train people to interpret Scripture carefully. The issue is not that second-category things exist. The issue is what happens when we mistake a useful historical form for the biblical definition of church – or when the third category begins distorting the first two.

title: Session 3
text:
How the methods developed
Most of the changes in church history happened for understandable reasons. The question is not who ruined the church. It is what happens when solutions accumulate across 2,000 years and eventually become our unconscious definition of what church is.







Era
What the church looked like




1st century
Jesus movement, household communities


2nd-3rd centuries
Increasing institutionalization: bishops, clergy, liturgy


4th century
Constantine, basilicas, professional clergy, large congregations


Medieval
Sacramental church, cathedral, priesthood, Mass


Reformation
Scripture recovered, pulpit elevated, sermon becomes central


Revivalism (1700s-1900s)
Preacher-audience model intensified


American voluntary church
Consumer choice, denominational competition


Modern evangelical church
Market-driven, programmatic, campus-based



The sermon is a useful example to trace in some detail, because it shows clearly how a method develops, becomes central, and eventually starts to define what “church” means in people’s minds.
In the New Testament, preaching and teaching are everywhere. Jesus preached. Peter preached at Pentecost. Paul preached extensively. But there is an important distinction between public proclamation of the gospel and what happened when an established congregation gathered. The Greek word kerysso – to proclaim or herald – frequently describes announcing the gospel to outsiders. Within gathered churches, the New Testament uses language of teaching, exhortation, prophecy, Scripture reading, and mutual participation. First Corinthians 14:26 says: “When you come together, each of you has a hymn, or a word of instruction, a revelation…” Colossians 3:16 says “teach and admonish one another.” The overall picture is more participatory than the modern sermon-centered service.
By around AD 150, something closer to a recognizable sermon is emerging. Justin Martyr describes Christians gathering on Sunday, reading from the memoirs of the apostles and the prophets, and then the president “verbally instructs and exhorts the congregation to imitate these good things.” Then prayer, then Communion, then care for the poor. It is beginning to look familiar – but the Eucharist still occupies a central place alongside the teaching.
By the third century, Origen is delivering systematic expository homilies on biblical books, and we still have large collections of his sermons. By the fourth and fifth centuries you have John Chrysostom – whose nickname literally means “golden-mouthed” – Augustine of Hippo, Ambrose of Milan, and Gregory of Nazianzus. Extended exposition of Scripture by a recognized clergy member is now firmly established.
Constantine’s legalization of Christianity in AD 313 matters here too. Christians increasingly gathered in large basilicas rather than in homes and smaller spaces, and that physical shift had consequences. A gathering of 20-50 people in a home accommodates interaction naturally. A gathering of hundreds or thousands in a basilica naturally encourages a clergy-to-congregation flow rather than a believer-to-believer one. The architecture started shaping the theology.
The biggest step toward the modern Protestant service comes in the 16th century Reformation. Luther, Calvin, Zwingli, and the other Reformers reacted against a medieval Catholic worship structure centered heavily on the Mass and dramatically elevated the proclamation and exposition of Scripture. In many Protestant churches the pulpit became visually dominant. Revivalism in the 18th and 19th centuries intensified the preacher-audience model further, and the modern evangelical service – worship music plus a 30-45 minute sermon as the principal event – is the result of that long development.







Period
What preaching looked like




AD 30-100
Apostolic proclamation, teaching, prophecy, participatory gatherings


AD 100-200
Recognizable homily emerging


AD 200-300
Regular expository preaching established


AD 300-500
Professional clergy preaching long sermons to large congregations


Medieval
Sermons continue; Eucharist-centered worship dominates


Reformation
Scripture exposition and sermon become the center of Protestant worship


Revivalism
Preacher-audience model intensified


Today
Worship music plus 30-45 minute sermon as primary event



The most honest conclusion is this: preaching is ancient and thoroughly Christian. Sermon-centered worship – where the extended monologue by a professional pastor becomes the organizing center of the weekly gathering – is much later. The interesting question is not whether the sermon is good. It often is. The question is how one particular form of teaching came to dominate the gathering so completely that many Christians now instinctively think that is what church is.
The same pattern applies to other elements. In many American churches today, “the pastor” means the primary preacher, the CEO, the organizational leader, the spiritual authority, and the public face of the congregation. That is not an obvious New Testament category. The word poimen – shepherd or pastor – appears as a ministry term most famously in Ephesians 4:11, but the far more common New Testament leadership language is elder (presbyteros) and overseer (episkopos), and these almost always appear in the plural. The development from elders among the congregation to developing clergy offices to the Reformation minister to the modern senior pastor spans centuries and was shaped by forces well beyond the New Testament text.
The building follows a similar arc. The earliest Christians met in homes for several centuries. By the third century they were adapting buildings specifically for worship – the Dura-Europos house church, dating to roughly AD 240, is an important archaeological example. After Constantine, large basilicas become Christian worship spaces and the architecture begins changing people’s understanding of what church is. Instead of “the church is gathering at Lydia’s house,” you increasingly get “the Christians are gathering at the basilica.” Eventually the building itself gets called the church. Language naturally evolves. But it can subtly shift theology.

title: Session 3
text:
Community logic versus organizational logic
This brings us to the current moment. Not all of what drives modern churches is ancient tradition. Some of it has been absorbed directly from contemporary American culture – specifically from consumer capitalism and organizational management.
Churches are not businesses. But they can unconsciously begin operating like them.



Community logic
Organizational logic




Belonging
Attendance


Formation
Programming


Participation
Consumption


Gifts
Roles


Relationship
Efficiency


Faithfulness
Growth


Disciple
Attendee


Shepherd
Executive


Mission
Brand


One another
Audience



Neither column is entirely good or bad. Churches inevitably have some organization, and organization is not inherently evil. The question is which logic is primary – which column actually drives decisions, structures, and how success gets measured.
A church operating primarily in the right column can develop a particular feedback loop: it produces religious experiences, attendees consume them, successful churches attract more consumers, increased attendance produces increased revenue, increased revenue funds better programs and facilities and staff, and better offerings attract more consumers. That is a very different feedback loop from the one the New Testament describes.
Consider the vocabulary that has developed for talking about church. “We need to attract young families.” “People really like our worship.” “We’re trying to grow attendance.” “What does your church offer for teenagers?” “We’re losing people to the church down the road.” None of those sentences necessarily indicates something terrible. But taken together they reveal a marketplace vocabulary. The congregation becomes a customer base. The church becomes a provider. The pastor becomes an executive. The worship team becomes content production. The sermon becomes the principal product. Programs become product lines. Attendance becomes market share.
When that logic takes hold, the third category begins distorting the first two. The methods start reshaping the functions, and the functions start obscuring the purpose.

title: Session 3
text:
The deeper question
Paul never conceptualizes people as going to the church. The people come together and thereby constitute the gathered church. That is a significant difference from how we talk today.
The New Testament’s scorecard for the church is not attendance, giving, number of campuses, size of staff, quality of programs, quality of preaching, or quality of music. Those things are not necessarily bad. Some may help accomplish the mission. But none of them is the mission.
The New Testament asks different questions. Are people becoming like Jesus? Are they loving one another sacrificially? Are barriers between people being overcome? Are ordinary believers being equipped to minister? Are the poor and vulnerable being cared for? Are people becoming disciples who make disciples? Does this community make the character of God visible to the surrounding world?
Those are much closer to what the New Testament actually cares about when it evaluates a church.

title: Session 3
text:
Questions worth sitting with

Using the purpose, functions, methods framework – what purpose does the Evangelical American Church seem to be organized around? What methods does it prioritize? Are those two things aligned?
Which column of community logic versus organizational logic feels more familiar from your experience? What are the implications?
Some of the discomfort people feel with church may not be rejection of the church at all. It may be grief over the distance between the church they long for and the church they have experienced. Does that distinction land for you?
What would a church actually look like that operated by community logic rather than organizational logic? Have you seen it? Is it realistic at scale?
